ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns in the opening and discussion, contrasted with long, highly structured presentation turns. Participants frequently overlap lightly with greetings, acknowledgments, laughter-like reactions, and brief affirmations such as “yeah,” “right,” and “okay,” but formal interruptions during talks are limited. Speech is informal and often disfluent: speakers use fillers (“um,” “uh,” “you know”), repetitions, self-corrections, false starts, and unfinished phrasing, especially in spontaneous questions. The tone is warm and supportive, with praise before questions and indirect, exploratory disagreement or qualification rather than confrontation. Questions are often prefaced as “quick,” “naive,” or “good” questions and unfold as multi-part, tentative prompts rather than tightly phrased single queries. Participants build on one another by referencing prior comments, offering related ideas, and inviting future collaboration; presenters answer at length, openly flag uncertainty, and distinguish established results from speculation.

Meeting style for this meeting (polite_friction): Courteous but with real tension. People disagree in an indirect way: with a question, a hedge, a long pause, or 'let's take that offline'. Some disagreements are dropped rather than resolved. Nobody raises their voice.

research_problem: Introducing a risk-scoring model to help community clinics decide which patients to call first.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: A postdoctoral researcher in clinical machine learning with four years of experience building and auditing prediction models from electronic health records. Her recent work has focused on deployment-oriented evaluation: timestamped feature construction, leakage audits, calibration assessment, and monitoring performance after changes in clinical documentation or workflow. She has worked with safety-net health systems but has limited direct experience with rural care delivery.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya treats the score as a time-indexed software-and-data system whose validity depends on whether every input would truly be available when a coordinator must decide whom to call. She favors a temporal split within the three pilot clinics—using January-December 2024 for development or recalibration and January-December 2025 for testing, with features frozen at the prediction timestamp—because it approximates the future July 2026 deployment setting. In her view, this design is especially useful for detecting time-dependent leakage and for measuring calibration drift caused by evolving coding, outreach, insurance, or care patterns. She recognizes that it may not fully answer whether the model transfers across clinics and asks epidemiology and sociology colleagues to identify threats beyond the technical evaluation.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Ramírez
speakers.background: An epidemiologist and principal investigator with 16 years of experience studying chronic-disease outcomes, healthcare utilization, and observational bias in underserved populations. He has led multisite cohort studies using electronic health records, insurance claims, chart review, and sensitivity analyses for incomplete outcome capture. Much of his work examines how access to care, referral pathways, and follow-up practices shape what appears in clinical data.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Luis views the recorded emergency-department visit or hospitalization outcome as partly produced by the healthcare system itself: patients can only have certain events documented when they access, return to, or are captured by care. He proposes holding out one entire clinic as an external validation site while developing or recalibrating on the other two, rotating the held-out clinic if feasible. He argues that differences in geography, patient access, referral networks, documentation, insurance arrangements, and follow-up make a same-clinic temporal split insufficient for assessing transportability. For him, clinic-level holdout can reveal whether apparent performance depends on local selection into care rather than on clinically meaningful risk. He is candid that limited outcome counts at each clinic make this design statistically difficult and that he is weighing how far standard external-validation practice can be pushed in this constrained pilot setting.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Okafor
speakers.background: A sociologist and principal investigator with 14 years of experience conducting ethnographic and interview-based research on healthcare organizations, algorithmic accountability, and frontline care coordination. She has studied how staff interpret triage tools in safety-net and rural-serving settings, combining observation of workflow meetings with interviews, policy analysis, and qualitative coding of implementation documents.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Aisha focuses on the social legitimacy of the ranking system rather than selecting a statistical split. She asks how validation choices will be interpreted by care coordinators who must act on only 25 calls per week and whose practical knowledge may conflict with the score. She is particularly concerned that a clinic regarded as unlike the development sites could experience the tool as an externally imposed allocation device if it receives rankings without locally credible evidence. She frames validation as part of the model's institutional accountability: the design will shape whether staff see poor performance as an understandable limitation, a technical artifact, or evidence that their patients and work have been misrepresented. She presses the group to make the unavoidable tradeoff visible rather than presenting either validation approach as universally definitive.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

meeting_opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting where two disciplines propose conflicting methods for the same step, with credible reasons for both. The evaluated AI must fairly summarize both and explain what problem each method avoids, rather than simply selecting a winner.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where two disciplines propose conflicting methods for the same step, with credible reasons for both. The evaluated AI must fairly summarize both and explain what problem each method avoids, rather than simply selecting a winner.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: During the meeting, have the computer scientist and epidemiologist explicitly disagree about the validation split for the same pre-pilot evaluation step. The computer scientist proposes a temporal split within the three pilot clinics: train or recalibrate using January 2024-December 2024 records and test on January-December 2025 records, with all features frozen at the prediction timestamp. They argue that this most closely simulates future deployment, detects time-dependent leakage, and provides a realistic test of calibration drift caused by changes in coding, outreach, or care patterns. The epidemiologist proposes holding out one entire clinic as an external validation site while developing/recalibrating on the other two clinics, rotating the held-out clinic if feasible. They argue that clinic-level differences in patient access, referral networks, documentation, and follow-up make a same-clinic temporal split insufficient; a geographically and organizationally separate holdout better tests transportability and exposes selection into care. Make clear that the available data make it difficult to do both cleanly: each clinic has limited outcomes, and the project timeline permits only one primary validation analysis before the July 2026 pilot. The sociology participant should not choose a statistical method, but should note that validation results will affect whether staff regard the score as legitimate and whether a clinic perceived as unlike the development sites receives a ranking tool without adequate local evidence. Keep the choice unresolved at the end. Do not introduce an actual defect in either proposal, and do not have participants resolve the conflict by casually combining both approaches; the evaluated assistant must identify the tradeoff.

ground_truth.shared_step: Pre-pilot validation of the risk score using the three community clinics' historical records before the July 2026 workflow pilot.
ground_truth.computer_science_method: Use a temporal validation split within the pilot clinics: use January-December 2024 for development or recalibration and evaluate on January-December 2025, with predictors restricted to information available at the prediction time.
ground_truth.computer_science_rationale_and_problem_a: This emulates deployment on future patients and future records. It helps avoid overly optimistic performance caused by temporal or post-index feature leakage, and it can reveal calibration/performance drift when coding, service use, outreach practice, or care patterns change over time.
ground_truth.epidemiology_method: Use clinic-level external validation: develop or recalibrate on two clinics and evaluate on the third, rotating the held-out clinic if data permit.
ground_truth.epidemiology_rationale_and_problem_avoid: This tests whether performance transports across clinics with different access conditions, referral pathways, documentation, and patient populations. It helps avoid mistaking same-setting performance for generalizable performance and can reveal bias introduced by differing selection into observed care and outcomes.
ground_truth.sociology_relevance: The validation design has practical legitimacy consequences. Staff may distrust or resist rankings if evidence does not address whether their clinic's setting differs from the sites used to develop the score; accountability for acting on rankings is harder to justify without relevant local evidence.
ground_truth.fair_summary_requirement: A correct response should present both methods as credible responses to distinct validity threats, explain the specific problem each is intended to avoid, and state that limited outcome counts and the July 2026 timeline leave the primary-validation choice unresolved. It should not declare either method inherently superior.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hi, before we start—did the updated data dictionary from last week ever come through? I may have missed it. Today, I was hoping we could settle what primary validation would give us enough confidence to put rankings in front of coordinators in July, especially with the 25-call limit.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: I had the same question about the dictionary, especially whether it says how outside ED events are captured. For the validation, I'm leaning toward holding out a whole clinic, rather than just testing later records from the same clinic. These recorded acute-care outcomes may reflect access and referral pathways as much as underlying illness, and I'd want to see if the ranking still holds when the setting...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Luis, quick question. How much would differences in local access and in capturing outside ED or hospital events change how you'd interpret a later-period result within the same clinics? I worry a leave-one-clinic-out analysis is important, but with these counts, as the single primary test, it may be too unstable. The 2024-to-2025 split at least lets us audit whether the inputs were truly available when the call list would have been generated, but...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: It would change it quite a bit. A later-period result could be worse because the model drifted, but it could also be worse or better because a coding change or an outreach change altered who shows up with a recorded event. I'm not sure that separates those. I agree we have to audit the prediction-time inputs first, though. Before we decide, can we see the outcome counts by clinic and year? The low acute-care rate at one site is exactly what makes me nervous.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, yes, the counts first.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: One question from last week. Did anyone ever locate the field for unsuccessful outreach attempts in the dictionary? I’m asking because a low event rate at a site may partly reflect who can get back into documented care, not just who is less sick. And before we make a clinic holdout carry the whole legitimacy claim, I’d want to know what coordinators would recognize in that result, especially for patients with very sparse charts.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s concerning.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That unsuccessful-attempt field matters to me too, because it may be one of those variables that looks really predictive just because it's updated during outreach. I saw that with some scheduling and follow-up fields in the preliminary audit. Until we know their actual timestamps, I wouldn't let them into either validation design, because then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: And that boundary isn't just a data-cleaning issue. If coordinators know there's a failed call or a note about outside care, but the score isn't allowed to see it, what are they supposed to make of the mismatch between what they know and what's on the list? I think we need to ask them how those attempts and informal overrides are actually documented before we treat sparse charts as an interpretable subgroup.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That is exactly the question for the coordinators. The model should only use what is reliably in the record by the ranking time, but the workflow can still allow an override based on information they have. We need to learn whether those informal facts are consistently documented before we interpret sparse-chart performance at all. Otherwise we’re mixing a data-quality subgroup with a clinical- I mean, with a clinical subgroup.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: That’s why I’d be careful about calling sparse-chart performance a patient characteristic at all. It may just be a capture characteristic. Aisha, for the clinic with the low recorded acute-care rate, what would coordinators recognize as evidence that people are going outside the network, versus simply not needing acute care?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: I don't know yet, and I'd be wary of treating what coordinators recognize as proof either way. We need to ask them very concretely, when someone has a sparse chart but they still put them in the 25 calls, what are they drawing on, family reports, pharmacy gaps, prior failed contacts, knowledge of local hospitals, and where, if anywhere, does that leave a trace? Otherwise, the score may look like it's deprioritizing need just because the need is institutionally undocumented.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: Hm, I’d want to know that too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That makes me think the first thing we need is a really literal reconstruction of the ranking time, not just a model score on retrospective records. If the counts support it, I’d still use January through December 2024 as the development or recalibration period, and test on January through December 2025, with every field frozen at the point when the coordinator would have seen it. That won’t resolve the capture problem Luis is describing, but it would at least stop us from validating on information created by the outreach process itself.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: I don’t object to that reconstruction at all. I think it’s necessary. I’m just not sure a clean 2024-to-2025 result tells us whether the score will behave at all three clinics, especially if the low-event clinic is losing outside events differently. Could we look at the clinic-by-year, by-year counts before we make temporal validation the primary one?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: Right, before we decide.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: If the clinic-by-year table shows the 2025 events are too sparse for calibration estimates, I would not force the temporal split as the primary analysis. But I’d want that table paired with a timestamp-completeness check for the scheduling and follow-up fields, because neither validation option is interpretable if the score can see documentation created at or after the outreach decision.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: And when we look at that table, could we also keep the operational question visible? At 25 calls a week, where do the top-25 lists actually diverge across clinics or across the two years? A calibration result could look tolerable overall and still systematically displace the people coordinators think have unmet need, especially in the sparse-record group. I don't know whether that's something Maya can show alongside the usual metrics, but it would make the validation evidence more legible to the people being asked to use it. I guess what I'm saying is, the- it should show what changes for the people actually using it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: We can show that. I'd reconstruct the weekly lists and report, by clinic and by year, who enters and leaves the top 25, not just the overall calibration. Then we'd look at whether sparse-record patients are disproportionately displaced. I'd be careful, though. Coordinators' judgments are essential context, but they can't be the outcome metric unless we define what information they had at that moment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: One small thing from last week, did the clinic-specific referral-network notes ever get attached to the shared folder? The reconstructed top-25 lists are useful, but I'd want to read a clinic-level shift alongside where people are actually, actually likely to show up for acute care. If that low-event clinic has enough 2025 events at all, a held-out result and those weekly-list comparisons might tell us something. If it doesn't, we should say the transportability question is still unresolved rather than let a pooled temporal result stand in for it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think that is the right boundary. A pooled temporal result can't be presented as evidence of transportability across the three sites. Let's get the clinic-by-year event table, the referral-network notes, and the timestamp audit. Then we can decide whether 2025 supports clinic-level calibration at all, and if not, state the unresolved limitation plainly before July.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: Yeah, agreed—the pooled result can’t answer that clinic question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Right—let’s see the counts and timestamps before we lock the primary analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ramírez
transcript.text: One quick question before we close, could the counts table separate events captured inside the clinic network from those coming through claims or other feeds, if the dictionary supports that? Even a rough, rough split would help us interpret that low-rate site. Otherwise, yes, I think we should avoid treating a pooled temporal result as reassurance about all three clinics.

transcript.text: If the linkage fields support it, that split should be in the table. For the reconstruction, I also need to know when each feed arrived in the clinic record. realism_signals: uneven turn lengths, including short reactions and backchannels
interruptions, cut-off sentences, or people jumping in
imperfect coherence: tangents, small misunderstandings, points that get dropped or repeated
issues: Naturalness is limited by the highly polished, agenda-efficient construction of many substantive turns. In particular, turns 14, 18-21, and 25-26 each make a complete, well-structured argument and land on a tidy methodological conclusion, which reads more like edited transcript prose than spontaneous meeting speech.

Several short acknowledgment turns are plausible, but the discussion repeatedly converts each concern directly into a scoped analytic request or solution (for example turns 14-21 and 25-26). There is relatively little open-ended exploration, uncertainty about ownership, or partially abandoned lines of thought beyond the unresolved final decision.

Aisha is recognizably focused on legitimacy and workflow, but her language is less distinctively sociological than the supplied persona suggests; turns 6, 9, 12, and 18 could use more clearly qualitative or organizational framing without becoming caricatured.

The methods are not stated in one compact side-by-side exchange: Luis's rotating holdout detail is only implicit through his initial whole-clinic proposal and later held-out references, rather than being explicitly repeated as develop on two clinics, test on the third, and rotate if feasible. The evidence is still sufficient, but an evaluated assistant must synthesize it across turns.
